content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

1	<!-- The text of the teaching page "Arrays in Fortress", written on 2026-11-17 by delegated Opus workers of the coordinating session for Pavol, the curator, at his questions on arrays after climb batch 33 was planned. Part 1, the language and the interpreter: how an array is written and typed, which part is syntax and which library, how the nat sizes ride in the type, where the elements live; every program ran under walk in a scratch worktree seeded from the base build at c3b16ef2d1 and removed after. Part 2, the compiled path, added at his word that his questions were mainly how arrays will run compiled: which classes the code generator writes for the library's arrays, how the class loader makes an instance's class, what a[i] and a[i] := v compile to layer by layer in real bytecode, where the boxes are made and where the JIT removes them, each way on file to an unboxed store and to unboxed arithmetic in terms of those classes, the walls between main and a compiled array program, and the transaction checks; its compiled code came from a second scratch worktree seeded from the same base build, with probe Y's selector and the rehearsal's marked hacks, nothing of it on main, removed after. No timing was taken. -->
2	
3	*Fortress revival · a teaching page · 17 November 2026*
4	
5	# Arrays in Fortress
6	
7	You asked how arrays work, and mainly how they'll run on the compiled path. Part 1 teaches the language and the interpreter, from small programs run under walk. Part 2 follows two of those programs into JVM bytecode, compiled against the one library, and from that bytecode to the design: where the boxes are, what each way to unbox would change, and what stands before a compiled array program runs on `main`. Each program on the page ran today, and its output is shown as it printed.
8	
9	## 1. The short answers
10	
11	**The language and the interpreter**
12	
13	- **Half language, half library.** The literal `[1 2 3]` and the shorthand `ZZ32[3]` are the language’s. The types behind them, `Array1`, `Vector` and `Matrix`, are the library’s.
14	- **The sizes ride in the type on both paths.** Walk checks them as a line runs. The compiled checker checks them before the compile.
15	- **Every element today is boxed**, a number wrapped in a heap object. The bare-double store that “nothing chooses” is the team’s immutable `RR64` array: no factory returns it.
16	
17	**The compiled path**
18	
19	- **The compiler makes the library’s arrays as it makes any library code.** Each generic trait and object becomes one template class. The class loader makes the class of each instance, such as `__DefaultVector⟦FRR64,1000⟧`, the first time a program uses it, with the sizes in its name. Where a body reads a size, the loader writes in the number.
20	- **`a[i] := v` is 11 calls deep.** The subscript operator, a bounds check against the size, the vector, the primitive array, the store’s trait, a generated wrapper, a Java helper, and the Java store, which asks whether a transaction is open. A read adds a cast.
21	- **Each element is an `FRR64` box in an `Object[]`.** Once a loop is hot, the JIT can remove a temporary box, where it inlines the whole chain down to it. It can’t remove an element’s box, or the box assigned to a mutable variable each iteration.
22	- **Five ways on file give a number array an unboxed store, and three say where the arithmetic runs on bare doubles.** Only the class loader’s way, the team’s direction, changes no library line, and nothing of it exists: the team left an empty stub in the loader and an unused plan.

80	## 3. The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s
81	
82	You took the array types for library types, and the literals for built-in syntax. Both are right. The language, its parser and walk, give:
83	
84	- the literal, `[1 2 3; 4 5 6]`, and the shorthand `T[n, m]`;
85	- the subscript forms `a[i]`, `a[i, j]` and `a[i] := v`;
86	- static parameters, `[\T, nat n\]`, where `nat` marks a size that the type carries.
87	
88	The library gives:
89	
90	- `Array[\E, I\]`, with no size in its type. `I` is the index type: `ZZ32`, or a pair for rank 2.
91	- `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Array2` and `Array3`, with a lowest index and a size for each dimension.
92	- `Vector` and `Matrix`, for numbers only, with their arithmetic.
93	- the factories `array1[\T, n\]()`, `vector`, `matrix`, and `array[\T\](n)` for a size known only when the program runs.
94	- the subscript itself: `a[i]` calls the operator `opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i))`, as Swift’s `a[i]` calls the type’s `subscript`.

96	They meet at two names that walk knows: `Array` plus the rank, and `__builtinFactory` plus the rank. For `[1 2 3]` at a declared type, walk calls `__builtinFactory1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]()` and copies the elements in. A literal with no declared type isn’t built today.

108	## 4. How the sizes ride in the type
109	
110	The library’s rank-1 array keeps no length field. It reads the size from its type:
111	
112	```
113	trait ReadableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] ...
114	    opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0
115	    offset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
116	        r = i - b0
117	        if NOT (0 <= r < s0) then oops(1, b0, s0, i) end
118	        r
119	    end
120	```

122	A product names a shared size once, so the shapes must match. An n-by-m matrix times a vector of m gives a vector of n:

124	```
125	opr juxtaposition[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n, nat m\]
126	    (me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], v: Vector[\T,m\]): Vector[\T,n\]
127	```

194	## 5. Where the elements live today
195	
196	A `Vector[\RR64,3\]` from `array1` is three objects deep. The vector, `__DefaultVector`, holds a `PrimitiveArray`. That holds a store, a `JavaArrayStore`. The store holds the elements in Java. A 2-by-3 matrix holds one store of `s0 s1` cells, 6, row by row: a size can be a product.
197	
198	- **Under walk**, the store is walk’s own `AtomicArray` of walk’s boxed values.
199	- **Compiled against the one library**, it’s the Java class `FortressArrayStore`, an `Object[]` of boxes such as `FRR64`. Inside `atomic`, each read and write of an element goes through the transaction. Section 7 follows one read and one write down to it.
200	- **Compiled against the prelude**, the compiler’s own small library, which `main` still uses by default, there’s no array type at all: “Array1 is undefined”.
201	
202	**The store over a bare double array** is in `PrimImmutableRR64Array`, the team’s immutable `RR64` array in the one library’s `NativeArray`. Walk holds its elements in a `double[]`, and so does its compiled class, `FortressRR64ArrayStore`. It has `get` and `init`, no `put`. “Nothing chooses it” means this:

204	```
205	im = immutableArray1[\RR64,3\]()
206	typecase im of
207	  PrimImmutableRR64Array[\3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the double[] store")
208	  PrimImmutableArray[\RR64,3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the general store")
209	  else => println("immutableArray1 chose something else")
210	end
211	r = PrimImmutableRR64Array[\3\]()
212	r.init0(0, 1.5)
213	r.init0(1, 2.5)
214	r.init0(2, 0.25)
215	println("the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = " (r[0] + r[1] + r[2]))

218	```
219	immutableArray1 chose the general store
220	the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = 4.25
221	```

223	The store works, and the factory doesn’t pick it. How a factory picks each element type’s store is your first open question.
224	
225	**The prelude’s native arrays are something else.** The prelude has `ZZ32Vector`, over a Java `int[]`, and `StringVector`, over a `String[]`. The team wrote both by hand in August 2011. They have no type parameters, no size in the type and no `RR64` version. A `for` loop can’t run over one, and neither can be a type argument. Each read returns a new boxed `ZZ32`: the storage is unboxed, the traffic boxed. They go with the prelude, which is deleted at the switch-over.

264	**The library’s classes.** The code generator writes one jar for each component. For each trait it writes a JVM interface, and a class of the trait’s bodies, the springboard, `T$DefaultTraitMethods`. A body there is a static method that takes the object first, and an object’s class gets small forwarders to it. For each object it writes a class. For a trait, object or function with static parameters, it writes a template instead: a class file with empty brackets in its file name, and beside it a `.xlation` file that lists the static parameters. `ReadableArray1⟦⟧`’s list says that `T` is a type and that `b0` and `s0` are sizes. `FortressLibrary`’s jar holds 1.6K classes and 0.9K lists. The array family, cut:
265	
266	```
267	FortressLibrary$ReadableArray1⟦⟧        trait: interface template
268	FortressLibrary$ReadableArray1⟦⟧$DefaultTraitMethods
269	FortressLibrary$Array1⟦⟧, $Vector⟦⟧     and their springboards
270	FortressLibrary$__DefaultVector⟦⟧       object: class template
271	FortressLibrary⚙$array1⟦⟧…              generic function: template
272	FortressLibrary$JavaArrayStore          no static parameters: plain
273	NativeArray$PrimitiveArray⟦⟧            in NativeArray’s jar
274	```
275	
276	**An instance’s class, made at first use.** No file is named `__DefaultVector⟦FRR64,1000⟧`. The first time `Dot` runs a line that names it, the JVM asks the Fortress class loader for it, and the loader:
277	
278	1. sees the brackets in the name, and cuts off the stem;
279	2. reads the template and its list;
280	3. copies the template’s bytes with ASM, a Java library for class files, putting `FRR64` for `T` and `1000` for `s0` in every name, descriptor and constant;
281	4. defines the result as a class. It never writes it to disk.
282	
283	C# makes a class per value type in this way; Java erases. A flag of the run saved the made classes for this page: 269 for `Dot`, 153 for `Arr`. `Dot` made `Array1⟦X,0,1000⟧` for all eight number types: `array1`’s `typecase` tests the element type against one arm after another, `RR64` last, and each test loads its arm’s classes. `Arr`, at `ZZ32`, the first arm, made only `Array1⟦FZZ32,0,8⟧`.

285	**The sizes, three ways.**
286	
287	- **In the name.** `1000` is part of the class’s name, as Swift mangles a type into a symbol. Two sizes give two classes.
288	- **As a descriptor**, the object that stands for a static argument when a type is tested as the program runs. A size’s descriptor is one shared object per number. The template reads a placeholder; the instance builds the real one once, when its class starts:
289	
290	```
291	// template PrimitiveArray⟦T,s0⟧, static {}
292	getstatic     PrimitiveArray⟦T,s0⟧$RTTIc.ONLY
293	// instance PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,1000⟧, static {}
294	getstatic     FRR64$RTTIc.ONLY
295	ldc           "1000"
296	invokestatic  RTTIsize.of(String)RTTI
297	invokestatic  PrimitiveArray$RTTIc.factory(RTTI,RTTI)RTTI
298	```
299	
300	- **As a value.** `PrimitiveArray` reads `s0` to make its store, `mem: JavaArrayStore = makeJavaArrayStore(s0)`. The template calls a placeholder, and the loader writes the number in, as a boxed `ZZ32`:
301	
302	```
303	// template, the constructor
304	invokestatic  CONST.Nat⟦s0⟧()FZZ32
305	invokestatic  FortressLibrary.makeJavaArrayStore(FZZ32)FJavaArrayStore
306	// instance ⟦FRR64,1000⟧, the constructor
307	ldc           1000
308	invokestatic  FZZ32.make(I)FZZ32
309	invokestatic  FortressLibrary.makeJavaArrayStore(FZZ32)FJavaArrayStore
310	```

312	That’s your picture: sizes stamped into a class. Nothing uses the constant as an `int` yet. Each read of `s0` makes a new box, as the bounds check in section 7 shows.

430	## 8. Where the boxes are made, and where the JIT removes them
431	
432	A boxed number is held in a heap object. On the compiled path an `RR64` is an object of the Java class `FRR64`, with one `double` field: Java’s `Double` against `double`. The code generator boxes every number, so `Dot`’s own code holds no `dadd` or `dmul`. The multiply `a[i] b[i]` is three calls down to one `dmul`, between two unboxes and a box:
433	
434	```
435	// FortressLibrary.juxtaposition(FRR64,FRR64): the dispatch method
436	invokeinterface RR64.juxtaposition☞0(FRR64)FRR64
437	// RR64$DefaultTraitMethods.juxtaposition☞0, a builtinPrimitive body
438	invokestatic    native.…simpleDoubleArith.doubleMul(FRR64,FRR64)FRR64
439	// the wrapper
440	invokevirtual   FRR64.getValue()D                    // twice
441	invokestatic    simpleDoubleArith.doubleMul(DD)D     // dload_0; dload_2; dmul; dreturn
442	invokestatic    FRR64.make(D)FRR64
443	```
444	
445	The second loop’s body, cut:
446	
447	```
448	// Dot$fn@11.apply(FZZ32 i):   s += a[i] b[i]
449	invokestatic    BaseTask.inATransaction()Z           // reading s
450	invokevirtual   MutableFValue.getValue()Any
451	invokeinterface Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧._[_](FZZ32)FRR64      // a[i]
452	invokeinterface Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧._[_](FZZ32)FRR64      // b[i]
453	invokestatic    FortressLibrary.juxtaposition(FRR64,FRR64)FRR64
454	invokestatic    FortressLibrary.+(FRR64,FRR64)FRR64
455	invokestatic    BaseTask.inATransaction()Z           // writing s
456	invokevirtual   MutableFValue.setValue(Any)V
457	```
458	
459	One iteration of that loop makes these boxes:
460	
461	- in the range’s own loop, which keeps its index in a mutable cell too: the `1` of `i += 1`, and the new index, which the cell keeps;
462	- in each of `a[i]` and `b[i]`: none for the element, which the store holds already, but four in the bounds check;
463	- the product, from the wrapper;
464	- the sum, which `s`’s cell keeps.
465	
466	That’s two boxes kept and ten dropped, each iteration. In the first loop, `asFloat(i)` and `1.0` each make a box that the array keeps: a literal is `FRR64.make` at every run.
467	
468	**Where the JIT removes a box.** Once a loop is hot, C2, the JVM’s optimizing compiler, inlines the dispatch, the wrapper, the helper, `make` and the box’s constructors. Escape analysis then drops each box that nothing keeps, such as the product’s. It needs that whole chain inlined, and C2 stops at a depth of 16 by default. In the prelude’s measured loops, a box’s last constructor sat 10 to 12 calls below the loop. Here the bounds check’s `-` is already 6 calls below the range’s loop, and the one library’s springboards chain longer than the prelude’s. So by count, my reading, the bounds check’s boxes sit near or past the limit, and may stay. Not measured.
469	
470	**Where it can’t.** An element’s box: the `Object[]` keeps it, so it escapes, 24 bytes an element plus its reference. The boxes of `s` and of the range’s index: each cell keeps its box, 24 and 16 bytes an iteration. And any box that crosses a call C2 doesn’t inline.
471	
472	**What the boxes cost.** Java models of the compiled boxes, against `double[]`: a dot product over 4K elements, 6.3 times; a 16-by-16 matrix product, 6.5 times; the row lift, a function applied to each row, 2.6 times. An `Object[]` behind an interface, with a cast on each read, added only 1.6 to 9 %: the boxes cost, the generic container doesn’t. A `double[]` store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box: a dot product over a `double[]` read through a boxing accessor ran at 8.9 times the bare loop, against 6.4 for boxed storage. So where the elements live and where the arithmetic runs unboxed are two decisions.
473	
474	**“Boxed numbers now”** means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, an object without identity that no type can extend. In the batch’s second run, rung N makes the prelude’s seven number types so, and the code generator writes each one’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value, a payload class: `FRR64` keeps its `double`, and the class of `RR64` extends it. The boxes stay the same boxes. What changes is that a value whose static type is `RR64` can only be that class, which unboxing by static type needs (section 10). For arrays that changes no decision. In your words: “All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.”

522	## 10. The ways to an unboxed store, and to unboxed arithmetic
523	
524	Your decisions set the goal and leave the way open. Unboxed doubles, and arrays of them, are required: “If this should have been high performance language, it cannot be boxed.” Every number type’s array is to be stored in a Java array of its primitive type, `double[]` first, with the sizes kept in the types. Each number type is one value object, so that compiled code can hold a bare `int`, `long` or `double`. Decision A, how a number type’s array gets its unboxed store, and decision B, where the arithmetic runs unboxed, are open, with no default, for after the switch-over. Their preparation, such as this page, comes before.
525	
526	**What every store way but A4 needs first.** The tree has a Java store over `double[]`, `FortressRR64ArrayStore`, with its helpers and its library trait. It lacks a `put`, since the team’s only `RR64` array is immutable; a carrier on the compiled path, which only the rehearsal’s hack has; and a mutable Fortress object written for `RR64` alone. With them, layers 5 to 8 of section 7 run over a `double[]`. The read’s wrapper already exists, for the immutable array, and the scratch tree compiled it:
527	
528	```
529	// native.com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.arrayOps.getRR64
530	invokevirtual   FJavaRR64ArrayStore.getValue()FortressRR64ArrayStore
531	invokevirtual   FZZ32.getValue()I
532	invokestatic    nativeHelpers.arrayOps.getRR64(FortressRR64ArrayStore,I)D
533	invokestatic    FRR64.make(D)FRR64                  // a new box at each read
534	```
535	
536	So the element lives bare, and each read makes a box at layer 6, which the JIT can drop if it inlines the reader. A write would unbox `v` with `getValue()` and store a `double`. Layers 1 to 4 stay as they are: their descriptors say `FRR64`.
537	
538	**Decision A, the store:**
539	
540	- **A1, the library’s own type test in the factories.** `array1`’s `typecase` already tests the element type to return a vector. Its `RR64` arm would return a vector object written for `RR64`, through the library’s `cast`: one more template, made as `__RR64Vector⟦1000⟧`, a size and no type in its name. `Dot`’s `invokeinterface Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧` stays; the class behind it changes. The cost is one type test per array made, and, at the first array of each size, the classes of each arm tested, eight for `RR64` (section 6). A probe checked and ran this shape on both paths, in the prelude’s world. The team: Jan Maessen, 2008, of the immutable `RR64` array: “these should be used in preference to the boxed version”.
541	- **A2, a plain `RR64` factory beside the generic one, chosen by dispatch.** The code generator writes a dispatch method for the pair, as for any overload; the store classes are A1’s. It compiled and dispatched in a probe. Walk refuses the pair at load today.
542	- **A3, a factory name for each element type**, `rr64Vector[\s0\]()`. No test at all: the call makes `__RR64Vector⟦1000⟧` directly. The model must name it, and `vector[\RR64,s\]` stays boxed.
543	- **A4, the class loader makes an `RR64` instance’s class with a `double[]` field.** The team’s direction, and your lean: “I would try to pursue the team’s direction unless we have a clear reason not to go there.” No library line changes and nothing selects. Making `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,1000⟧`, the loader would write a class whose `mem` is a `double[]`, with `daload` and `dastore` in `get` and `put`. Today it only renames: a field of type `T` becomes `LFRR64;`, and `[D` is no class name. So A4 is new work in the loader and in the code generator, which must mark the templates that can be made so and give them the bodies that renaming can’t. Nothing of it exists and no probe has run. What the team left: the loader’s branch for it, `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }`, empty since 2009; and David Chase’s plan, `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`, 250 lines that list what to unbox (a primitive such as `RR64` as a `D`, an object without fields, unboxed fields, a `comprises` of unboxable types) and that nothing calls. A4 also needs one name per number type at run time, where the record finds two today, the interface’s and the box class’s. Even with A4, a read through the `Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧` interface returns an `FRR64`, unless decision B changes the descriptor.
544	- **A5, a special type**, an `RR64Vector` that the code generator lowers to a hand-written Java class, as it lowers `ZZ32Vector` to `FZZ32Vector` over `int[]`. No type parameter, no size in its type, not in the specification, and the model names it. It goes against the sizes in the types.

547	
548	- **B1, Java helpers over whole arrays.** `Vector`’s `dot` would bind a helper that loops over two `double[]` in Java: one call per whole operation, plain Java inside. FACTS.md:286
- F-388 **The compiler's prelude declares its seven number types as value objects, whose classes the code generator writes over the run time's payload classes.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64` are `value object`s in `CompilerBuiltin`; each object's class extends the abstract payload class `compiler/runtimeValues/F<T>`, which holds the JVM value. So a program's object below a number type is refused at the compile, an overloading at `ZZ32` beside one at a program's trait is valid, a `typecase` clause at such a trait over a number is refused as unreachable (row 1081), and a number type named as a value does not compile (row 1082). The words that this section uses:
- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** checks a program with the **checker** and then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**.
- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses by default. The **one library** is the library of the interpreter.
- The **selector** is the setting `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. With it, the compile command reads the one library. A program compiled so does not run yet.
- A **value object** is an object with value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Nothing can extend an object.
- A **payload class** is a small hand-written Java class that holds the bare JVM number, such as an `int`. The code generator writes each number object's class on top of it.
- A **row** is one known defect in the ledger. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.
- The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.
- A **task** is one change of the run. The record names it a rung. A **worker** is an agent that does one task. A **skeptic** is a second agent that examines the worker's change. A **judge** is a third agent that rules where the skeptic contests a fix.
- A **fork** is a design question with more than one way. A **default** is the way that the record chose before the run.
- A **varargs parameter** takes any number of arguments, written `xs: ZZ32...`.
- A **type assumption**, `e asif T`, makes the call around it choose its declaration as if `e` were a `T`.
- An **arm** is one clause of a `typecase`.
- The **measure** counts the declarations of the one library that the code generator refuses.

**What each task changed.** Each program is shortened from the tests that landed.

- **N. The prelude's seven number types are value objects.** The prelude, the code generator and seven run-time classes changed.

content.content:
Fortress revival · a teaching page · 17 November 2026

Arrays in Fortress

You asked how arrays work, and mainly how they'll run on the compiled path. Part 1 teaches the language and the interpreter, from small programs run under walk. Part 2 follows two of those programs into JVM bytecode, compiled against the one library, and from that bytecode to the design: where the boxes are, what each way to unbox would change, and what stands before a compil

Sections

  1. The short answers

Part 1. The language and the interpreter

  1. An array, written and typed
  2. The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s
  3. How the sizes ride in the type
  4. Where the elements live today

Part 2. The compiled path

  1. What the compiler makes of an array program
  2. a[i] and a[i] := v, layer by layer
  3. Where the boxes are made, and where the JIT removes them
  4. What the rehearsal ran, and why its loop was slow
  5. The ways to an unboxed store, and to unboxed arithmetic
  6. From main to an array program that runs compiled
  7. The transaction checks

Closing. Your decisions, and the reports to read

  1. Your design questions
  2. The deeper reports

1The short answers

The language and the interpreter

  • Half language, half library. The literal [1 2 3] and the shorthand ZZ32[3] are the language’s. The types behind them, Array1, Vector and Matrix, are the library’s.
  • The sizes ride in the type on both paths. Walk checks them as a line runs. The compiled checker checks them before the compile.
  • Every element today is boxed, a number wrapped in a heap object. The bare-double store that “nothing chooses” is the team’s immutable RR64 array: no factory returns it.

The compiled path

  • The compiler makes the library’s arrays as it makes any library code. Each generic trait and object becomes one template class. The class loader makes the class of each instance, such as __DefaultVector⟦FRR64,1000⟧, the first time a program uses it, with the sizes in its name. Where a body reads a size, the loader writes in the number.
  • a[i] := v is 11 calls deep. The subscript operator, a bounds check against the size, the vector, the primitive array, the store’s trait, a generated wrapper, a Java helper, and the Java store, which asks whether a transaction is open. A read adds a cast.
  • Each element is an FRR64 box in an Object[]. Once a loop is hot, the JIT can remove a temporary box, where it inlines the whole chain down to it. It can’t remove an element’s box, or the box assigned to a mutable variable each iteration.
  • Five ways on file give a number array an unboxed store, and three say where the arithmetic runs on bare doubles. Only the class loader’s way, the team’s direction, changes no library line, and nothing of it exists: the team left an empty stub in the loader and an unused plan.
  • The first array program to run is the smallest of the switch-over rehearsal, a trial in a throwaway tree. The switch-over moves the compiled path, the compile to JVM bytecode, onto the one library, the interpreter’s library. The program makes an array of 8 ZZ32 with the library’s factory, writes i i into each element, and prints a[5] = 25You need to do nothing now. An array is library code: Fortress traits and objects over a store, the object that holds the elements. The open array decisions are about speed and the model’s own types, not about running.
  • The rehearsal’s loop was about 100 times slower than Java. Boxing explains 6 to 7 of that. The rest has no measured share.
  • Boxed numbers now change no array decision. A bare-double store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box.
References
  1. The program, its compile and its run: CLIMB-BATCH-33.md, section 2, “R. A method found by its interface”, “The measures” and “For the batch after, in this order”, item 4. The compiled path: sections 6 to 12, from a scratch tree with hacks. The rest: the sections below.

Part 1

The language and the interpreter

Small programs run under walk, the interpreter: what an array is, in the language and in the library.

2An array, written and typed

Start from the specification’s example, with a few lines added. typecase takes the first arm whose type matches the value as it runs, like Swift’s switch with case is T.

A: ZZ32[3,3] = [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]
println("A[1,0] = " A[1,0])
println("|A| = " |A|)
v: RR64[3] = [1.0 2.0 3.0]
println("v DOT v = " (v DOT v))
typecase v of
  Vector[\RR64,3\] => println("v is a Vector[\\RR64,3\\]")
  else => println("v is no vector")
end
s: String[2] = ["ab" "cd"]
typecase s of
  AnyVector => println("s is a vector")
  Array1[\String,0,2\] => println("s is an Array1[\\String,0,2\\], no vector")
  else => println("s is something else")
end

Under walk, it printed:

A[1,0] = 4
|A| = 9
v DOT v = 14.0
v is a Vector[\RR64,3\]
s is an Array1[\String,0,2\], no vector
  • Spaces separate the elements of a row. A semicolon or a new line separates rows, and two semicolons separate the planes of a 3-dimensional array.
  • ZZ32[3,3] is the specification’s shorthand for Array2[\ZZ32, 0, 3, 0, 3\]: for each dimension, a lowest index, 0, and a size, 3. That’s the notation on the number type that you saw.
  • A[1,0] is row 1, column 0, counted from 0.
  • One literal syntax gave a matrix, a Vector and a plain Array1. The specification lets the context decide. The library’s factory decides, by testing the element type against the eight number types.
  • The overview’s RR^3, a vector of 3, isn’t built. Walk reads it as a type of its own. Today v: RR64^3 = [1.0 2.0 3.0] bound, and the println(v) after it stopped: “Couldn’t figure out Matrix [\RR64\]^(3) <: Object”.
References
  1. The literal, its type and the shorthand: aggregate.tex, lines 117 to 137; the example, Expr.Array.a.fss.
  2. The context decides, and T^n: overview.tex, lines 735 to 773 and 934 to 938; Overview.Expression.aggregate.a.fss, FortressLibrary.fss, lines 2842 to 2856; FACTS F-229.
  3. T^n under walk: gap ledger row 24. The stopped println is today’s run, a shape that the row doesn’t name.
  4. The run: Literal.fss, by bin/fortress in a worktree seeded from the base build at c3b16ef2d1, whose library equals main’s at 9f2ff9b04e.

3The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s

You took the array types for library types, and the literals for built-in syntax. Both are right. The language, its parser and walk, give:

  • the literal, [1 2 3; 4 5 6], and the shorthand T[n, m];
  • the subscript forms a[i], a[i, j] and a[i] := v;
  • static parameters, [\T, nat n\], where nat marks a size that the type carries.

The library’s classes. The code generator writes one jar for each component. For each trait it writes a JVM interface, and a class of the trait’s bodies, the springboard, T$DefaultTraitMethods. A body there is a static method that takes the object first, and an object’s class gets small forwarders to it. For each object it writes a class. For a trait, object or function with static parameters, it writes a template instead: a class file with empty brackets in its file name, and beside it a .xlation file that lists the static parameters. content.content:
• The first array program to run is the smallest of the switch-over rehearsal, a trial in a throwaway tree. The switch-over moves the compiled path, the compile to JVM bytecode, onto the one library, the interpreter’s library. The program makes an array of 8 ZZ32 with the library’s factory, writes i i into each element, and prints a[5] = 25. After the second run of climb batch 33, the next launch, it compiles against the one library on main. It runs in the batch after, once that library compiles whole to bytecode. In this page’s scratch tree, with hacks, it ran, and so did the dot program (section 6).

    • “Boxed numbers now” means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, an object without identity that no type can extend. In the batch’s second run, rung N makes the prelude’s seven number types so, and the code generator writes each one’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value, a payload class: FRR64 keeps its double, and the class of RR64 extends it. The boxes stay the same boxes. What changes is that a value whose static type is RR64 can only be that class, which unboxing by static type needs (section 10). For arrays that changes no decision. In your words: “All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.”

  • Value objects: POSITIONS P-178; the payload class, carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md, “Way C”, form 2, and “Way D”; the rung: CLIMB-BATCH-33.md, “N. The prelude’s seven number types become value objects”; the phase: PLAN.md, “Phase 6. microGPT fast”.
  • A4, the class loader makes an RR64 instance’s class with a double[] field. The team’s direction, and your lean: “I would try to pursue the team’s direction unless we have a clear reason not to go there.” No library line changes and nothing selects. Making PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,1000⟧, the loader would write a class whose mem is a double[], with daload and dastore in get and put. Today it only renames: a field of type T becomes LFRR64;, and [D is no class name. So A4 is new work in the loader and in the code generator, which must mark the templates that can be made so and give them the bodies that renaming can’t. Nothing of it exists and no probe has run. What the team left: the loader’s branch for it, if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }, empty since 2009; and David Chase’s plan, compiler/optimization/Unbox.java, 250 lines that list what to unbox (a primitive such as RR64 as a D, an object without fields, unboxed fields, a comprises of unboxable types) and that nothing calls. A4 also needs one name per number type at run time, where the record finds two today, the interface’s and the box class’s. Even with A4, a read through the Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧ interface returns an FRR64, unless decision B changes the descriptor.
  • B2, unboxing by static type in generated code. Wherever the checker’s type is RR64, the code generator keeps a JVM double: s a double, a[i] b[i] a dmul, f(x: RR64): RR64 a method of descriptor (D)D. It boxes only where the value meets Any, a trait above RR64, or a type parameter. In Dot, the loop’s own arithmetic becomes dmul and dadd, but the library’s generic code still sees T: the read through Array1⟦FRR64,…⟧ still returns a box, unless A4, or a store object written for RR64, gives it a D descriptor. It needs the closed number types of your value-object decision, rung N’s payload classes, and a second set of descriptors, which the team named in a comment in NamingCzar and never built. It’s the team’s precedent, Unbox.java’s first case, and the largest code-generator work in the plan.

    • 11From main to an array program that runs compiled

    A rung is one change, which one worker builds and a second checks. A run is one launch of a batch’s rungs. The gate is the full check before a run lands.

    Run 1 of climb batch 33, landed on 17 November. FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one makes the compile command read the one library. A println program then compiles, and doesn’t run: the library has no bytecode yet. Arr still stops in the code generator: “Not in the trait table: Array1”, since a method entry names the trait without its interface file.

    Run 2, next, on your same go. Rung R finds a trait’s methods by the interface file that declares it, so Arr compiles, and its jar names Array1⟦FZZ32,0,8⟧ and seq⟦FZZ32⟧, as the scratch tree’s did. Other rungs compile varargs, which println uses, give two hidden functions on one line two class names, and make the prelude’s number types value objects. Five programs then compile against the one library. None runs: fortress run Arr dies at its first library class, “NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/FortressLibrary$String”.

    The batch after, wall by wall, in the classes of section 7:

    1. The carriers. A carrier is the Java class that holds a built-in type’s values. The wrapper for arrayOps can’t be written, since nothing carries JavaArrayStore: FortressArrayStore is a plain Java class, outside the Fortress types. Each built-in type needs its class for the one library: the two stores, Boolean, Char, the flat string, the reader, the writer, and the seven number types by rung N’s form. The wrapper also needs converters for a helper’s Java String and Object: arrayOps.get returns an Object, which must arrive as Any. And the run time’s 105 exception names still name the prelude.

    2. The declarations that the code generator refuses. One refused declaration stops its component’s jar. After run 2, by the planner’s probe, 1 or 2 are left, Generator2 and perhaps CatString, and NN32’s two getters, declared at Number, stop FortressBuiltin. Then the 14 compiles write the library’s jars, and Hello runs under the gate.

    3. The run tests of varargs and of the class names.

    4. The walls only a running program shows, in the order the rehearsal met them:

      • the dispatch method FortressLibrary⚙$seq⟦FZZ32⟧ names its component without the package fortress, so the first for dies, “NoClassDefFoundError: FortressLibrary”;
      • seq takes its element type from the range’s descriptor, which names ZZ32’s interface, where compiled code names FZZ32, so it makes a Generator⟦ZZ32⟧ that the range isn’t: “ClassCastException”;
      • the code generator writes one method twice into 27 of the library’s classes: “ClassFormatError: Duplicate method name”;
      • the JVM’s verifier refuses methods of the library itself, so every program dies as the library’s class loads: on the rehearsal’s base QQ’s, which wait for a cast that the code generator doesn’t emit yet; in this page’s scratch tree simplestRationalBetween first. The rehearsal, probe Y and this page ran with the verifier off.

      Then Arr and Dot become tests. Here the array program runs.

    5. Smaller code-generator rows and the checker’s other gaps.

    6. The matrix and the library’s DOT as tests, then what microGPT needs from the checker.

    Then the switch-over ends: the compiled tests move, and the prelude is deleted. Next comes the phase in which microGPT compiles, with its static types and the array design, then the phase in which it runs fast.

    This page’s scratch tree. It started from the base build at c3b16ef2d1 and took probe Y’s patch, which holds the rehearsal’s hacks. 25 of its 28 files applied as they stand. Its three library files didn’t: they make Float, RR32, NN32, Boolean and Char traits with carrier objects, and Float is gone since your value-object decision. In their place, the tree made each of the nine built-in value objects, ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ, NN64, RR64, NN32, RR32, Boolean and Char, a trait over one empty object, so that the hand-written box classes can extend their springboards. It typed NN32’s two getters NN32, and dropped Float from the carrier tables. Then:

    • the build passed, and the one library’s 14 components compiled, each with exit 0;
    • the tolerant code generator left 11 declarations out: assert, deny, __filter, __bigOperator2 and Generator2 of FortressLibrary; List, app and <|_|> of List; concatAndBalanceIfNecessary and stringifyChars of String; APPCOV;
    • Arr and Dot compiled, and ran with the verifier off;
    • with the verifier on, Arr dies as FortressLibrary’s class loads: “VerifyError: Bad local variable type”, in simplestRationalBetween, a function with label and exit, which the code generator compiles since the rehearsal. No ledger row names it.

    No other wall stopped it.

    References

    3. The run’s walls: switch-rehearsal.md, W2, W6, W7, W11 and W12; probe-y.md, sections 3 and 4; plan-33/PROBES.md, sections 6 and 11.
    4. The scratch tree: probe-y.patch, applied with its three library files left out and redone as above; the verifier’s refusal, bin/fortress run Arr without the rehearsal’s flags.

> <!-- The text of the teaching page "Arrays in Fortress", written on 2026-11-17 by delegated Opus workers of the coordinating session for Pavol, the curator, at his questions on arrays after climb batch 33 was planned. Part 1, the language and the interpreter: how an array is written and typed, which part is syntax and which library, how the nat sizes ride in the type, where the elements live; every program ran under walk in a scratch worktree seeded from the base build at c3b16ef2d1 and removed after. Part 2, the compiled path, added at his word that his questions were mainly how arrays will run compiled: which classes the code generator writes for the library's arrays, how the class loader makes an instance's class, what a[i] and a[i] := v compile to layer by layer in real bytecode, where the boxes are made and where the JIT removes them, each way on file to an unboxed store and to unboxed arithmetic in terms of those classes, the walls between main and a compiled array program, and the transaction checks; its compiled code came from a second scratch worktree seeded from the same base build, with probe Y's selector and the rehearsal's marked hacks, nothing of it on main, removed after. No timing was taken. Part 2 brought up to date on 18 November 2026, after climb batch 33b landed at ba3c7c876d, from the record alone. -->
> - **The first array program to run** is the smallest of the switch-over rehearsal, a trial in a throwaway tree. The switch-over moves the compiled path, the compile to JVM bytecode, onto the one library, the interpreter’s library. The program makes an array of 8 `ZZ32` with the library’s factory, writes `i i` into each element, and prints `a[5] = 25`. Since the second run of climb batch 33 landed, on 18 November, it compiles against the one library on `main`. It runs in the batch after, once that library compiles whole to bytecode. In this page’s scratch tree, with hacks, it ran, and so did the dot program (section 6).
> *Brought up to date on 18 November 2026, after climb batch 33b, run 2 of climb batch 33, landed.*
> 
> Every compile, run and listing in this part came from a scratch tree with hacks: a throwaway worktree, seeded from the base build at `c3b16ef2d1`, with probe Y’s selector and the rehearsal’s marked hacks put in, and removed after. Nothing of it is on `main`. On `main` today, `Arr` compiles against the one library, and no program runs there yet (section 11).
> **“Boxed numbers now”** means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, an object without identity that no type can extend. Run 2 of the batch made the prelude’s seven number types so. The code generator now writes each one’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value, a payload class: `FRR64` keeps its `double`, and the class of `RR64` extends it. The boxes stay the same boxes. What changes is that a value whose static type is `RR64` can only be that class, which unboxing by static type needs (section 10). The one library’s seven take this form later, in the task where the first program runs on the one library: the default of fork N4, one of the batch’s design questions. Until then, in a run against the one library, a payload class’s `make`, such as the `FZZ32.make` of section 6’s listing, stops with an error that names the missing form. For arrays that changes no decision. In your words: “All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.”
> 4. Value objects: POSITIONS P-178; the payload class, [carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md), “Way C”, form 2, and “Way D”; the rung: [CLIMB-BATCH-33.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-33.md), “N. The prelude’s seven number types become value objects”, landed: FACTS F-388; the one library’s seven: [rung N’s report](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-number-payload-objects/REPORT.md), “The one library’s seven (fork N4, a point to report)”; the phase: [PLAN.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md), “Phase 6. microGPT fast”.
> - **A4, the class loader makes an `RR64` instance’s class with a `double[]` field.** The team’s direction, and your lean: “I would try to pursue the team’s direction unless we have a clear reason not to go there.” No library line changes and nothing selects. Making `PrimitiveArray⟦FRR64,1000⟧`, the loader would write a class whose `mem` is a `double[]`, with `daload` and `dastore` in `get` and `put`. Today it only renames: a field of type `T` becomes `LFRR64;`, and `[D` is no class name. So A4 is new work in the loader and in the code generator, which must mark the templates that can be made so and give them the bodies that renaming can’t. Nothing of it exists and no probe has run. What the team left: the loader’s branch for it, `if (false) { // Here will go all the magic expando-stuff. }`, empty since 2009; and David Chase’s plan, `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java`, 250 lines that list what to unbox (a primitive such as `RR64` as a `D`, an object without fields, unboxed fields, a `comprises` of unboxable types) and that nothing calls. A4 also needs one name per number type at run time. Since run 2, each of the prelude’s seven has one, its payload class’s, such as `FRR64`; the one library’s seven get it with fork N4. Even with A4, a read through the `Array1⟦FRR64,0,1000⟧` interface returns an `FRR64`, unless decision B changes the descriptor.
> - **B2, unboxing by static type in generated code.** Wherever the checker’s type is `RR64`, the code generator keeps a JVM `double`: `s` a `double`, `a[i] b[i]` a `dmul`, `f(x: RR64): RR64` a method of descriptor `(D)D`. It boxes only where the value meets `Any`, a trait above `RR64`, or a type parameter. In `Dot`, the loop’s own arithmetic becomes `dmul` and `dadd`, but the library’s generic code still sees `T`: the read through `Array1⟦FRR64,…⟧` still returns a box, unless A4, or a store object written for `RR64`, gives it a `D` descriptor. It needs the closed number types of your value-object decision, which rung N built for the prelude and fork N4 brings to the one library, and a second set of descriptors, which the team named in a comment in `NamingCzar` and never built. It’s the team’s precedent, `Unbox.java`’s first case, and the largest code-generator work in the plan.
> 6. How a number type’s class holds a bare value: [carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md), “Way C”, “Way D”, “Way H” and “Way I”; as built for the prelude: FACTS F-388, gap ledger row 995.
> **Run 1 of climb batch 33, landed on 17 November.** `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` makes the compile command read the one library. A `println` program then compiles, and doesn’t run: the library has no bytecode yet. After it, `Arr` still stopped in the code generator: “Not in the trait table: Array1”, since a method entry named the trait without its interface file.
> 
> **Run 2, which the record calls climb batch 33b, landed on 18 November, at `ba3c7c876d`.** Rung R finds a trait’s methods by the interface file that declares it, so `Arr` compiles. Its test, `OneLibraryArray1`, is `Arr` with an `assert` for its print, and every gate compiles it. Rung G compiles a varargs parameter, one that takes any number of arguments, such as the last parameter of the library’s `assert`. Rung W gives two hidden functions on one line two class names, and rung N makes the prelude’s number types value objects (section 8). Nine programs now compile against the one library, in the gate’s track for `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. None runs: the one library has no jars yet, so a run dies at its first library class, “NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/FortressLibrary$String” (row 1062). No rung of run 2 answers an array question: the array design’s questions and decisions A, B and D stay open (section 13).
> 
> A varargs parameter is an array. In
> 
> ```
> count(xs: ZZ32...): ZZ32 = |xs|
> ```
> `xs` is an `ImmutableArray[\ZZ32, ZZ32\]`, a write-once array. For `count(4, 5, 6)`, the compiled call makes an `ImmutableArray1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]` with the library’s factory `__immutableFactory1`, and fills it in order with `init`, as walk does. Against the prelude, which has no array type, the code generator still refuses a varargs parameter.
> 2. **The declarations that the code generator refuses.** One refused declaration stops its component’s jar. The measure counts them, with hacks that pass the carriers and `NN32`’s getters: 13 before run 2, and 1 after it, on `ba3c7c876d`. The one left is `__bigOperator2` (row 1076), the library’s function for one big operator nested in another, where a generic method is called on a value whose type is a type variable. `Generator2` and `CatString` now compile. `NN32`’s two getters, declared at `Number`, still stop `FortressBuiltin` (row 993). Then the 14 compiles write the library’s jars, and `Hello` runs under the gate.
>    - `seq` takes its element type from the range’s descriptor, which names `ZZ32`’s interface, where compiled code names `FZZ32`, so it makes a `Generator⟦ZZ32⟧` that the range isn’t: “ClassCastException”. Rung N’s form names a number type by its payload class at run time too, so by reading, not by a run, this wall goes with fork N4;
> - with the verifier on, `Arr` dies as `FortressLibrary`’s class loads: “VerifyError: Bad local variable type”, in `simplestRationalBetween`, a function with `label` and `exit`, which the code generator compiles since the rehearsal. Row 1078 now records it.
> 1. [CLIMB-BATCH-33.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-33.md), section 2: “Run 1, rung by rung”, “Run 2, rung by rung”, “The measures”, “What still stands before the first program runs on the one library”, “For the batch after, in this order”. Run 2 as landed: [batch-33b-review.md](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/batch-33b-review.md), “For the curator”; FACTS F-388 to F-391; the selector, F-381. The measure: [measure-ba3c7c876d.txt](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/compile-ladder/plan-33/probes/measure-ba3c7c876d.txt), against `measure-d3747846c1.txt` beside it.
> 2. Gap ledger rows 1062, no run yet; 874, the carriers; 993, `NN32`’s getters; 994, the dispatch’s package; 995, the two names; 307, the cast; 1076, `__bigOperator2`; 1078, the verifier’s refusal; and, closed, 1061, `Arr`’s stop, 624, varargs, 315, the class names, and 81, `label`. The tests: `one_library_tests/OneLibraryArray1` and `OneLibraryVarargsCount`. The factory: [FortressLibrary.fsi](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/Library/FortressLibrary.fsi#L1795-L1798), lines 1795 to 1798. The phases: POSITIONS P-33.
> Written on 17 November 2026 for the curator, from the record and the tree at `main` `9f2ff9b04e`. Part 1’s programs ran under walk in a scratch worktree seeded from the base build at `c3b16ef2d1`, removed after. Part 2’s compiled code came from a second scratch worktree seeded from the same base build, with probe Y’s selector and the rehearsal’s marked hacks, nothing of it on `main`, removed after. No timing was taken. Part 2 was brought up to date on 18 November 2026, after climb batch 33b’s landing, from the record at `main` `4bcc1d8b81`; nothing was run for it. The same text, as a note for the record: `arrays-primer.md`.
